mechanism_steps.mechanism: head-level pruning leaves factual recall paths intact
accuracy is stable until redundancy is exhausted

claim: When does structured pruning reduce inference cost while preserving factual accuracy?

h1.headline: Prune the parts that are redundant for factual recall first.
h1.how_to_check: Run matched head-first and MLP-first ablations at the same sparsity and latency budgets, then compare factual QA accuracy.

key_terms.plain_meaning: removing whole model components rather than individual weights
whether answers preserve factual claims under evaluation

h1.status: This is a testable idea, not a proven conclusion.
h1.what_might_be_happening: Some attention heads may duplicate routing information, while MLP channels may carry entity-specific facts that factual QA needs.
h1.what_would_change_our_mind: The idea weakens if MLP-first pruning preserves factuality equally well at matched latency.
h1.why_it_matters: The result would turn structured pruning from a generic compression knob into a safer target-selection policy.

h2.headline: A factuality cliff may mark the useful pruning limit.
h2.how_to_check: Sweep pruning ratios across benchmarks and fit piecewise curves for latency and factual accuracy.

key_terms.plain_meaning: the point where factual accuracy starts falling faster than latency improves

h2.status: This is a testable idea, not a proven conclusion.
h2.what_might_be_happening: Pruning may improve latency smoothly while factual accuracy stays stable only up to a threshold, then drops quickly.
h2.what_would_change_our_mind: The idea weakens if accuracy declines linearly with no detectable threshold.
h2.why_it_matters: A threshold curve would help choose compression ratios that save inference cost without silently sacrificing factuality.
